notes: Demanding path whose correct end state is an unresolved family. The need names two designs with intent cues (a retrospective records comparison and a randomised comparison), so routing is unresolved at create; the problem reply returns family null (issue 'cleared', basis stays unresolved, D2). The recorded fixture search returns HTTP 200 with zero records. The only scan reply (shape discovery, no items) proposes certainty 'moderate' and also carries a key investigatorConfirmsEmptySearch: the certainty is dropped with an issue, the key is dropped with an issue and no confirmation is stored, and the stage stays incomplete ('not assessed', no 'moderate certainty' label; G1, G2, D20). The investigator then confirms the empty search on screen, which completes the stage with certainty still unassessed. The design reply recommends null on purpose: design.recommended stays empty and basis unresolved (D2), and its 'defer' decision rests on no claim (nothing was retrieved) and on one gate met by the investigator's approval ACM-2026-14; acceptance is therefore accepted with the action ready, and no family is set (recommendedFamily null). A reload on the Design route follows the acceptance and a reopen follows the last stage. Unlike an empty search followed by a later successful search, this path never retrieves a record and never assigns certainty. No record ids exist in this scenario (the only search is empty). Requires D2 (null family and null recommendation keep basis unresolved), D20 (no certainty and no completion over zero records, the model confirmation key dropped, investigator confirmation, 'not assessed'), S11 (routing at create, recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (decision status text). Catches: a certainty label over an empty search, a model field that confirms an empty search, a null recommendation that leaves a stale family or basis, and a defer decision refused or blocked without reason.

inputs.need:
I am the lead pharmacist for a hospital-run anticoagulation clinic that manages about 1,150 patients on warfarin, most with atrial fibrillation or a mechanical heart valve. Two dosing approaches are in use at the same time. Pharmacists at the main site adjust doses with a paper nomogram based on the latest INR, while the two satellite clinics switched last year to a computer-assisted dosing tool built into the clinic software, which suggests a weekly dose from the last three INR values. Nobody has compared them. Our medical director wants to standardise on one approach by next spring, and the satellite pharmacists are convinced the software keeps patients in range for longer.

I am not sure how to answer this. We could do a retrospective comparison of time in therapeutic range using the clinic records for patients managed under each approach, but the satellite clinics see younger patients with fewer interacting medicines, so the groups are not alike. Or we could plan a randomised comparison where new referrals are allocated to one approach or the other, which would take much longer and needs the pharmacists at the main site to learn the software. I also do not know whether our INR records are complete enough to calculate time in range: results from home testing are sometimes entered late or not at all.

I need help deciding what can honestly be done, what the outcome should be (time in range, or bleeding and clot events), and whether we should settle the design now or check the data first.
inputs.constraints: No research funding. Pharmacist time for data work is limited to about four hours a week. Patient-identifiable clinic records may not leave the hospital network. Any change to dosing practice needs approval from the anticoagulation committee.

The clinic manager approved a four-week profile of INR and dose records for completeness on 2026-09-08 (approval ACM-2026-14).
Home point-of-care INR results are entered by clerical staff, and the delay between test and entry is not recorded anywhere.

response.statement: Two warfarin dosing approaches run side by side in one anticoagulation clinic: a paper nomogram at the main site and a computer-assisted dosing tool at two satellite clinics since October 2025. The medical director wants to standardise by next spring, but the approaches have never been compared, the sites differ in case mix, and it is not known whether the INR records are complete enough to calculate time in therapeutic range. response.whoAffected: About 1,150 adults on warfarin, many older and on interacting medicines, the clinic pharmacists at three sites, and the anticoagulation committee that must approve any change.
response.whatHurts: Time outside the therapeutic range raises the risk of bleeding and of stroke or valve thrombosis; standardising on the wrong approach, or on the right one for the wrong reasons, would affect every patient in the clinic.
response.currentPractice: Main site: dose adjusted from the latest INR with a paper nomogram. Satellites: weekly dose suggested by the dosing tool from the last three INRs and confirmed by the pharmacist. Home test results are entered by clerical staff with unrecorded delay.
response.whyNow: Standardisation is planned for next spring, and the satellite pharmacists' confidence in the software has not been tested against the clinic's own data.
response.constraints: No research funding. Pharmacist time for data work is limited to about four hours a week. Patient-identifiable clinic records may not leave the hospital network. Any change to dosing practice needs approval from the anticoagulation committee.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Every patient spends as much time as possible in the safe INR range with the fewest dose changes and clinic contacts, whichever approach the clinic keeps.
response.summary: Problem framed; the design family is left unresolved because both candidate designs depend on data whose completeness is unknown.

response.overview: Two-step plan. Step 1 (October 2026): a four-week profile of INR and dose records at the three clinics to establish whether time in therapeutic range can be calculated. Step 2 (from January 2027, only after the design decision is revisited): either a records comparison adjusted for case mix or a randomised comparison of new referrals, with the primary outcome fixed now so that it cannot drift with the design.
response.population: Step 1: every patient on warfarin managed by the clinic during the profile window (about 1,150). Step 2: adults starting or continuing clinic-dosed warfarin at any site, excluding patients who self-manage their dose at home.
response.exposure: Dose adjustment with the paper nomogram (main site) or with the computer-assisted dosing tool (satellites).
response.procedures: Step 1: a pharmacist extracts, for each patient, the dates of INR tests, the dates of entry where known, the doses recorded, the testing mode (clinic or home) and four case-mix variables (age, indication, interacting medicines, time on warfarin), inside the hospital network. Time in range is counted as calculable when no gap between INRs exceeds 56 days. Step 2 is specified after the decision is revisited against criterion k1.

outcomes.name: Time in therapeutic range
outcomes.measure: Percentage of days with INR in the target range, by linear interpolation between consecutive INRs, per patient
outcomes.timing: 26 weeks from the start of step 2
outcomes.why: The standard measure of dosing quality that either design can use; fixed before the design is chosen.

outcomes.name: Major bleeding or thromboembolic event
outcomes.measure: Hospital attendance for major bleeding, stroke or systemic embolism
outcomes.timing: 26 weeks from the start of step 2
outcomes.why: The outcome patients care about; too rare to power at clinic scale, so reported descriptively.

outcomes.name: Calculability of time in range
outcomes.measure: Proportion of patients with no INR gap longer than 56 days, by clinic and testing mode
outcomes.why: Decides whether the records comparison is possible (criterion k1).

outcomes.name: Pharmacist time per dosing decision
outcomes.measure: Minutes per dosing decision timed on 40 decisions per approach
outcomes.why: Standardising must not add workload the clinic cannot absorb.

response.feasibility: Step 1 needs about 16 hours of pharmacist time over four weeks, within the four hours a week available, under approval ACM-2026-14; the feasibility of step 2 depends on the design chosen after the profile.

response.theoreticalFramework: None; a data-quality profile followed by a comparative design chosen on a pre-stated rule.
response.summary: Records profile first, with the comparison's primary outcome fixed in advance; the design stays open by decision.

response.designSummary: Step 1 is descriptive. Step 2 has two candidate analyses, both specified now so the design choice cannot change them.
response.sampleSize: Step 1 includes every patient in the four-week window (about 1,150); if 70 percent have calculable time in range, the 95 percent confidence interval is about plus or minus 2.6 percentage points, precise enough to apply criterion k1 at each clinic. For step 2, with a between-patient standard deviation of time in range of about 20 percentage points, detecting a 5-point difference with 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 needs about 252 patients per approach in a randomised comparison, about 17 months of the clinic's 30 new referrals a month. A records comparison could include about 600 patients per approach at once, but its precision would not protect it from confounding by site.
response.primaryAnalysis: Step 1: proportion of patients with calculable time in range by clinic and testing mode, with Wilson 95 percent intervals. Step 2, records comparison: linear regression of time in range on approach adjusted for the four case-mix variables. Step 2, randomised comparison: difference in mean time in range with a 95 percent confidence interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Major bleeding and thromboembolic events per 100 patient-years by approach, descriptive only; distribution of test-to-entry delay where recorded; minutes per dosing decision by approach.
response.missingData: Patients without calculable time in range are counted and described by clinic and testing mode, never imputed; any step 2 analysis restricted to calculable patients reports the restriction and its size.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome per step; secondary outcomes are descriptive and are not tested.
response.software: R, with extraction rules and analysis code archived before step 1 starts.
overfittingGuards: Outcome and case-mix variables fixed before any data are seen
Design chosen on calculability only, never on observed time-in-range values
Step 2 sample size fixed from the planning values stated here
response.summary: Step 1 estimates calculability to about 2.6 points; a randomised step 2 would need about 252 patients per approach.

response.risks: Step 1 carries minimal risk: a review of existing clinic records by clinic pharmacists inside the hospital network. Step 2 risks depend on the design; a randomised comparison changes how new patients are dosed and carries the usual risks of either approach.
response.consent: Step 1 uses records already held for care and needs no individual consent under the clinic's service evaluation approval. If step 2 is randomised, new referrals give written consent to allocation and may decline without any change to their care.
response.data: Extraction stays inside the hospital network; the analysis file holds a study number, clinic, testing mode, INR dates and values, doses and the four case-mix variables, with no names or health numbers.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older and rural patients, patients with limited English and patients with cognitive impairment are more likely to test at home and to have late or missing entries. Completeness is reported by testing mode and preferred language, and no design will quietly exclude patients whose records are incomplete.
response.effectiveness: The profile is worth doing if it decides the design; a finding that records are unfit is a useful answer that prevents a misleading comparison.
response.efficiency: About 16 pharmacist hours for step 1; step 2 costs are estimated only after the design is chosen.
response.costs: Pharmacist time within existing roles; no software or licence costs for step 1.
response.grants: None for step 1; a randomised step 2 could seek a regional pharmacy practice grant.
response.partnerships: Satellite and main-site pharmacists, the clinic manager, clerical staff who enter home results, and two patients who test at home.
response.rebPath: Step 1 is a service evaluation of record completeness under clinic approval ACM-2026-14; the hospital research office will be asked to confirm in writing that it needs no REB review. Step 2 requires REB review whichever design is chosen, following ICH-GCP principles.
response.limitations: The profile describes four weeks only and cannot show whether either approach is better; completeness may change once staff know it is being measured.
response.summary: Minimal-risk records profile with equity reporting by testing mode and language; REB review deferred to the chosen step 2 design.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patients who test at home and one satellite pharmacist review the profile's reporting categories before extraction; the clerical team explains how home results reach the record.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comment cards from the clinic waiting rooms over the last year are read for mentions of dose changes and home testing.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: I phone my result in on Monday and sometimes nobody calls back with a dose until Thursday.
items.implication: Record test-to-entry delay in the profile where it can be found, and report it by testing mode.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (satellite pharmacist): The tool is steadier than my own guesses, but I still override it for the patients who are ill or just back from hospital.
items.implication: Count overrides if step 2 compares the approaches.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (main-site pharmacist): If we have to learn the software in the middle of a busy clinic, the first months will not be a fair test.
items.implication: Plan a run-in period before any randomised comparison.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: Every new dose means a new pill pattern for my father, and that is when he gets it wrong.
items.implication: Report the number of dose changes alongside time in range.

response.summary: Four composite voices on delayed results, overrides, learning curves and dose-change burden.

response.title: Can warfarin dosing approaches be compared from clinic records? A pre-specified records profile and decision rule in a three-site anticoagulation clinic
response.abstract: Background: a paper nomogram and a computer-assisted dosing tool are used side by side in one anticoagulation clinic, and standardisation is planned. Methods: a four-week profile of INR and dose records at three clinics, with a pre-specified rule for choosing between a records comparison and a randomised comparison, and a primary outcome fixed in advance. Results and conclusions will be written after the profile.
response.introduction: Standardising dosing practice without local evidence risks choosing on enthusiasm. A recorded search for comparisons of these approaches in pharmacist-led clinics returned no records, and the clinic's own records have never been checked for completeness.
response.methods: All patients on warfarin in a four-week window; extraction of INR dates, entry dates where known, doses, testing mode and four case-mix variables inside the hospital network; calculability defined as no INR gap longer than 56 days; decision rule stated before extraction.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present calculability by clinic and testing mode, entry delays where recorded, and the design chosen under the pre-stated rule.
response.discussion: The discussion will state whether a records comparison is defensible, what the profile implies for patients who test at home, and what a randomised comparison would require.
response.limitations: Four weeks of data; completeness may improve while it is being measured; no comparison of dosing quality is made in this step.
response.conclusion: To be written after the profile; it will report fitness of the records and the design chosen, not which approach is better.
